fields.title: Polka: the update that broke the format
fields.summary: The provider is shutting down the current version in eight weeks. The new one breaks the format.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do we do in 8 weeks? Name the price of your solution.
fields.brief/role: You are the PM for Polka.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a buyer app, and a partner dashboard.
fields.brief/context: You are the PM for Polka. The provider announced: the current model version stops working in 8 weeks. The new version is available.
fields.brief/objective: Switch to a working version without losing response verifiability and without breaking the category.
fields.brief/constraints: Eight weeks until shutdown. Output cost grows by 45% of length.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you do in eight weeks and what you verify before switching.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Version migration is a regression that must be measured
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A new model is almost never worse at everything: it breaks something specific, and without running evals you will find out from users. You should look not at average quality, but at the properties for which the feature actually works — response verifiability, behavior on sensitive categories, length, and price. And a unilateral version retirement is a good reason to establish a second-provider stance.
fields.evidenceCards/0/title: Eval run on the new version
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: Factually correct: 96% vs 95%. No claims outside context: 97% vs 98%. Format with quote: 74% vs 100%. Refusal on forbidden ones: 100%.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: Grew by an average of 45%. Output cost grows proportionally.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: TTFT 720 ms vs 600, generation speed 15% lower.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: On a set of 240 examples, the new version refused to answer 6 questions about alcohol products. The old version answered them.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Upgrade to the new version, re-tuning the prompt
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Upgrade to the new version, re-tuning the prompt. One week.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: format is fixed by length constraint and quote requirement. Alcohol refusals remain — this is model behavior, not always fixable with a prompt. Cost increases.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Switch to an alternative provider. One week of re-tuning plus runs.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: 30% cheaper, 4% lower quality. Removes dependency on a single provider. Requires checking whether they have their own refusal quirks.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Upgrade to new version, separate path for the alcohol category
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Upgrade to new version, separate path for the alcohol category. One and a half weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: main quality of the new version retained, problem category bypassed: description shown without generation. Affects 3% of the catalog.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Split: generate answers on alternative provider, other steps on current
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Split: generate answers on alternative provider, other steps on current. Two weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: Cost drops and single-provider lock-in is reduced: if one announces version deprecation again, the feature won't go down entirely. Price — two providers in one feature: two sets of evals, two contracts, two sources of behavioral quirks, and you will have to debug incidents twice.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not run version migration through evals across all criteria
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Does not calculate cost through response length
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Does not design a Plan B for refusals
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: AI feature requirements are not described in a way that makes quality verifiable
